teaching.hint: Which decimal palindromes could never be prime, and how might the remaining candidates be visited in increasing order?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: Every even-digit palindrome is divisible by 11, except 11 itself can be prime; odd-digit palindromes can be generated from their leading half.
solution_outline.approach: Handle small one-digit answers and 11, then enumerate odd-length palindromes in increasing order from their leading halves. For each candidate at least `n`, test primality and return the first prime.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: The generated candidates are exactly the odd-length palindromes in increasing order; all excluded even-length values except 11 are composite.
solution_outline.correctness: Every possible prime palindrome is either handled in the small cases or visited by the generator, so the first qualifying prime is the minimum.
solution_outline.complexity: Up to answer value `V`, there are `O(√V)` generated candidates; trial division takes at most `O(√V)` per candidate, giving a conservative `O(V)` bound and `O(log V)` digit storage.
solution_outline.pitfall: Skipping 11 along with other even-length palindromes loses a valid answer.

common_wrong_turns: Test every integer from n upward
Assume all even-length palindromes are composite
source_fidelity_notes: The existence and answer-range guarantee is preserved.
